ui.faqIntro: Straight answers about travelling with AussieCamps.
ui.faq1a: AussieCamps is an iPhone app for finding places to camp and stay around Australia. It bundles a directory of 74,000+ places so the details stay readable without reception, and it turns the ones you save into a road trip with an ordered route, dates, notes and to-dos.
ui.faq2a: More than 74,000 places: campgrounds, caravan parks, roofed accommodation, farm and station stays, backpacker hostels, roadside rest areas, day-use areas, dump points, potable water, laundromats, information centres, long-vehicle parking, experiences and other useful stops.
ui.faq3a: The place directory is bundled with the app, so names, categories, descriptions, fees, amenities, opening hours and conditions stay readable well beyond signal. Live services such as weather, routing, Street View, photos and provider pages still need a connection.
ui.faq4q: Can I plan a multi-stop road trip?
ui.faq4a: Yes, and it is the app's main feature. Add places as stops, drag them into order, attach a date and arrival notes to each one, see the driving distance leg by leg and across the whole trip, open directions to the next stop, check the weather at each one, tick stops off as visited and keep the packing list beside the itinerary. Itinerary details can sync to Calendar.
ui.faq5a: Two kinds. Smart collections (Liked, Starred, Want to visit, Visited, Pins and All saved) fill themselves as you mark places. On top of those you can create your own named collections with an icon and notes for a region, a season, a vehicle or a shortlist.
ui.faq6q: Can I filter for free camps or caravan access?
ui.faq6a: Yes, and combinations of them. Filters cover category, fee type, minimum rating, online booking, state or territory, and detailed feature groups for access, amenities, activities, services and affiliations, so “free camping areas with toilets and drinking water in Queensland” is a single query.
ui.faq7q: What is on a place screen?
ui.faq7a: Photos, a description, opening hours, fees, terms and conditions, amenities and features grouped by type, current alerts, ratings, contact and booking details, weather, Street View where coverage exists, directions, and nearby alternatives.
ui.faq8a: A standard map and a satellite view built on Apple's flyover imagery, which you can tilt and rotate for real 3D terrain. Street View, built on Apple's Look Around imagery, gives the street-level view from the place screen.
ui.faq9q: Can I see prices in my own currency?
ui.faq9a: Yes. Choose your currency in settings and set the conversion rate, and reported fees are shown in that currency alongside the Australian dollar figure.
ui.faq10q: Can I book a campsite in AussieCamps?
ui.faq10a: Open the booking details for a place to reach its provider and check live availability, prices and terms.
ui.faq11q: Are camping rules the same across Australia?
ui.faq11a: No. Rules vary by state, territory, council, park and individual site. Always follow current signs, land-manager conditions, fire restrictions and official alerts.

support.title: How can we help?
support.lede: Clear answers for maps, saved places, trip planning and the road ahead.

sections.heading: Finding places
paragraphs: Use Explore to search by place name, address or description. Move the map and choose the current-area option to focus results around the visible region.

Filter by place category, fee, rating, online booking, state and detailed feature groups for access, amenities, activities and services. Combine only the filters that matter so useful alternatives remain visible.
Facilities, fees, access and management can change. Follow current signs and the land manager, then send a correction so the directory can improve.

sections.heading: Saved places
paragraphs: Liked, Visited, Want to Visit and Starred update automatically when you mark places. Pins and All Saved provide other quick views.
Create named collections with an icon and notes, then add any place. Use them for a region, season, vehicle or shortlist.
The app supports private iCloud sync for saved states, collections and trip data when iCloud is available and enabled.

sections.heading: Trip planner
paragraphs: Create a trip, add places and drag them into order. Each stop can carry its own arrival date, notes, weather and visited status, and the planner shows the driving distance leg by leg and across the whole trip.
Road routing depends on available MapKit directions. The planner retains the stops if a leg fails, but you must confirm current road access yourself.
Start with a camping essentials preset or make your own tasks. Trip progress keeps the list beside the itinerary, and itinerary details can sync to Calendar.

sections.heading: Maps, weather and live details
paragraphs: Switch between the standard map and a satellite view built on Apple's flyover imagery, which tilts and rotates into 3D terrain. Street View, built on Apple's Look Around imagery, opens from the place screen where coverage exists.
Current and forecast weather requires live data. Save critical forecasts and official warnings before leaving coverage.
The bundled place directory keeps core place details available beyond reliable signal. Live maps, routing, weather, photos and external provider pages may require reception.

sections.heading: Prices and currency
paragraphs: Choose your currency in settings and set the conversion rate. Reported fees are then shown in that currency alongside the Australian dollar figure, which helps when you are visiting and not fluent in AUD.
Open a place's booking or contact details to check availability, price and terms with the provider. Prices in the app are reported figures, not live quotes.

sections.heading: Premium and account
paragraphs: Map and place details are free, together with two saved lists.
Premium adds unlimited saved lists, trip planning, advanced filters, place weather and road trip routes.
Open the Premium screen and use Restore Purchases while signed into the Apple account used for the original transaction.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.lede: AussieCamps helps you plan a trip without turning your journey into an advertising profile.

sections.heading: Information stored on your device
paragraphs: Saved places, collection membership, trips, notes, checklist items and preferences are stored for the app to work. Location can be used to show your position and nearby places after you grant permission.

sections.heading: iCloud
paragraphs: When iCloud is available and enabled, the app can use your private iCloud database to sync saved states, collections and app records across your devices. Apple provides the underlying service and applies its own terms.

sections.heading: Live Apple services
paragraphs: Map display, directions, Look Around, weather, calendar integration and widgets may use Apple frameworks. Requests and data handling for those services are governed by Apple. Calendar access occurs only after permission and is used to add trip itinerary information you request.

sections.heading: External links and website logs
paragraphs: Place details can open booking providers, websites, social profiles, phone numbers, email addresses and map apps. Those services receive information according to their own policies when you choose to open them.

Hosting providers may process routine technical logs such as IP address, browser type and requested URL for delivery, reliability and security. AussieCamps does not use advertising trackers on this website.

sections.heading: Retention and control
paragraphs: You can delete app records through the app and manage iCloud data through your Apple account. Removing the app can remove local data, while synced copies may remain in iCloud until separately deleted.

sections.heading: Children and contact
paragraphs: AussieCamps is a general travel utility and is not directed to children. Do not submit personal information about a child through support.
For privacy questions, contact AussieCamps support.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.lede: AussieCamps is a planning aid. It does not replace official signs, land-manager directions, emergency warnings, road advice or your responsibility to travel within your capability.

sections.heading: Travel information changes
paragraphs: Places, prices, access, facilities, phone coverage, weather, fire conditions, roads and booking arrangements can change without notice. Verify critical details with the responsible authority or provider before travel and again close to departure.

sections.heading: No booking or access guarantee
paragraphs: A listing does not guarantee that a place is open, legal for your setup, reachable by your vehicle or available. External booking and contact links are provided for convenience. Contracts are between you and the third-party provider.

sections.heading: Safety and lawful use
paragraphs: You must obey signs, permits, closures, fire restrictions, road rules and directions from rangers, Traditional Owners, emergency services and land managers. Do not use the app while driving.

sections.heading: User data
paragraphs: You are responsible for notes, trip plans and other information you save. Keep separate copies of permits, bookings and safety-critical plans when loss of access could put a trip at risk.

sections.heading: Purchases
paragraphs: Any in-app purchase is processed by Apple and subject to the terms shown at purchase. Features, packaging and prices may change where allowed. Use Apple’s purchase tools for billing, cancellation and refund matters.

sections.heading: Intellectual property and contact
paragraphs: AussieCamps branding, interface and original editorial content belong to their respective owner. Place names and public facts remain the property or responsibility of their original sources.
Questions can be sent to AussieCamps support.

camping-rules-new-south-wales.title: Camping rules in New South Wales
camping-rules-new-south-wales.description: Bookings, designated sites, remote camps and fire checks before a night in NSW.
camping-rules-new-south-wales.imageAlt: National park campground in New South Wales
camping-rules-new-south-wales.intro: NSW camping rules depend on who manages the land. National parks, state forests, councils and private campgrounds each set their own conditions.

sections.heading: National park campgrounds
body: NSW National Parks requires advance bookings for listed campgrounds and hard-roof accommodation. Keep the confirmation available and enter the correct party and vehicle details.
Remote camping is allowed only in specific areas. A trip intention form may be recommended even where a standard campground booking is not used.

sections.heading: Free and roadside camping
body: A rest area is not automatically a campground. Read parking limits and council signs, keep truck bays clear and do not set up awnings or furniture where only a fatigue stop is intended.
Council reserves and showgrounds can have local permits, time limits or closures. Confirm them on the day.

sections.heading: Fire and park alerts
body: Check NSW park alerts, fire danger ratings and total fire bans before departure. A supplied fireplace does not make a fire legal during a ban.
Conditions can close parks with little notice. Keep a legal backup outside the affected area.

sections.heading: Who manages the land you are on
body: NSW splits camping between National Parks and Wildlife Service reserves, State Forests, Crown land, local council reserves and private property. Each has its own booking system, fees and rules, and the boundaries are frequently invisible from the road.

NPWS campgrounds are booked online and most charge both a camping fee and a separate vehicle entry fee for the park. State Forests are generally free and far less regulated, which makes them the practical option for dispersed camping.
Council reserves vary enormously between local government areas. A rest area that permits overnight stays in one shire will be prohibited in the next, and the signage is the only reliable guide.
tips: NPWS charges camping plus park entry
Council rules change at every boundary

sections.heading: Booking NPWS campgrounds
body: Popular coastal and mountain campgrounds book out months ahead for summer, Easter and school holidays, and walk-up availability is rare in those windows. Outside them, most sites can be booked a few days out.

An All Parks Pass covers vehicle entry to most NSW parks for a year and pays for itself quickly if you are visiting more than a handful. It does not cover camping fees or the Sydney Harbour and Kosciuszko parks in all cases.
Bookings are per site with a stated maximum occupancy and vehicle count. Turning up with more people or vehicles than booked is a common cause of trouble at busy grounds.
tips: All Parks Pass covers entry only

sections.heading: Fires and total fire bans
body: The NSW bush fire danger period usually runs from October to March and varies by local government area. During it, a permit is needed for most open fires, and on total fire ban days no open flame is allowed at all.
Solid fuel barbecues and campfires are prohibited on total fire ban days. Gas appliances are generally permitted subject to conditions, but check the specific ban wording because it changes.
Many NPWS campgrounds prohibit fires permanently regardless of the season. Check the individual campground page rather than assuming the state-wide position applies.
tips: Fire danger period October to March
No solid fuel on ban days

sections.heading: Free camping and rest areas
body: Transport for NSW rest areas are provided for driver fatigue management and many permit a stay of up to 24 hours, but they are not campgrounds and setting up awnings and chairs is not the intent.
Genuine free camping is most reliably found in State Forests, on some Crown land, and at council-designated sites, several of which ask for a small donation to the local community.
Enforcement varies but is real in coastal councils and popular areas. Fines apply for camping in prohibited areas, and the infringement attaches to the vehicle, so a rental company will pass it on.
tips: Rest areas are for fatigue, not camping
State Forests are the free option

sections.heading: Marine parks and coastal access
body: NSW marine parks apply zoning rules that restrict fishing and collecting in sanctuary zones, and the boundaries are published rather than signed on every beach. Check before fishing anywhere on the coast.

Beach driving is permitted in some areas with a permit and prohibited elsewhere. Stockton and parts of the mid north coast allow it, and the permits are issued by the relevant council or parks agency.
State forests remain the most flexible option in New South Wales, and the forestry agency publishes maps showing where camping and vehicle access are permitted.
An All Parks Pass covers vehicle entry across most NSW parks for a year and pays for itself quickly once you visit more than a handful.

camping-rules-queensland.title: Camping rules in Queensland
camping-rules-queensland.description: Permits, advance bookings and park alerts for Queensland parks and forests.
camping-rules-queensland.intro: Queensland protected-area camping usually starts with a permit. Book before arrival and carry the permit details beyond phone coverage.

sections.heading: Book and pay before arrival
body: Queensland requires a camping permit for national park and forest camping areas. Most permits are booked online, and popular places can fill weeks ahead during school holidays.
Display the camping tag as instructed. Vehicle access permits can be separate, particularly on recreation areas and islands.

sections.heading: Bush camps and vehicle access
body: Bush camping is allowed only where the park permits it. Stay away from waterways, tracks and picnic areas, and follow the specific low-impact conditions for the route.
K'gari and other sand destinations require vehicle preparation, tide knowledge and separate access checks. A two-wheel-drive map pin is not enough evidence of access.

sections.heading: Alerts, weather and fires
body: Check Queensland park alerts, Bureau of Meteorology warnings and fire bans before leaving. Wet-season roads and creek crossings can close quickly.
Never enter floodwater. Turn around and use the backup camp rather than waiting at an unsafe crossing.

sections.heading: National parks and the permit system
body: Queensland national park camping requires a permit booked in advance through the Queensland Parks system, and permits must be displayed. Many sites are remote, basic and have limited or no facilities.
Popular islands and coastal parks, including K'gari and the Whitsundays, book out months ahead and have specific vehicle and access requirements on top of the camping permit.
Some parks require a separate vehicle access permit, particularly for beach driving. Check both before travelling, because arriving with one and not the other is a common and expensive mistake.
tips: Permits must be booked and displayed
Beach driving needs a separate permit

sections.heading: Crocodile country changes the rules
body: Estuarine crocodiles are present from roughly Rockhampton northwards and in all tropical waterways including creeks, estuaries and beaches. Croc-wise signage is posted widely and should be treated as absolute.

Do not camp within about fifty metres of the water's edge in croc country, do not clean fish at the water, and never swim outside a designated safe area. Crocodile behaviour is not predictable from appearance or water clarity.
Report sightings to the relevant authority rather than assuming somebody already has. Removal of problem animals depends on reports, and it protects the next campers as much as you.
tips: Camp well back from the water

sections.heading: The wet season and road closures
body: Northern Queensland's wet season runs roughly November to April, bringing monsoonal rain, cyclones and widespread road closures. Many national park campgrounds close entirely for the season.

Unsealed roads become impassable quickly and driving them wet causes damage and attracts fines. Check closure status with the local council or the state road authority daily rather than relying on a forecast.
The dry season from May to October is when most of the state's camping works properly, and it is also when the popular sites fill with travellers escaping southern winters.
tips: Dry season fills with southern travellers

sections.heading: Free camping and council sites
body: Queensland has a strong network of council-run low-cost and free camping areas, many in small inland towns actively encouraging travellers to stop and spend locally. Stay limits are typically 24 to 72 hours.
Some require self-contained vehicles and most have specific signed conditions. Showground camping is also common and usually inexpensive with basic facilities.
Coastal council areas are considerably stricter than inland ones, reflecting demand. Assume that a beachfront car park is prohibited unless signage explicitly says otherwise.
tips: Showgrounds are a good cheap option

sections.heading: K'gari and dingo safety
body: K'gari has specific and strictly enforced dingo safety rules, including staying in groups, never carrying food while walking and using the fenced camping areas. Serious attacks have occurred and the rules exist because of them.
Feeding or leaving food accessible to dingoes carries substantial fines. Habituated animals are the ones that attack, and every incident traces back to food access.
Queensland's parks booking system opens a rolling window ahead of arrival, and the most popular island and coastal sites are taken within minutes of release.
Vehicle access permits for beach driving are separate from camping permits, and arriving with only one is a common and expensive mistake on the islands.

camping-rules-victoria.title: Camping rules in Victoria
camping-rules-victoria.description: Bookings, fees, seasonal roads and fire restrictions across Victoria.
camping-rules-victoria.intro: Victoria has bookable national park campgrounds, free basic sites and commercial parks. The exact campground page is the only reliable place to confirm fees and facilities.

sections.heading: Bookings and campground conditions
body: Book Parks Victoria sites through the official system where required. Bring the vehicle registration and keep the confirmation accessible.
Some camps are first come, first served, while others close seasonally. Do not occupy a booked or closed site because it appears empty.

sections.heading: State forests and roadside stops
body: Camping in state forests follows different rules from national parks. Use established sites, protect waterways and check local firewood and fire restrictions.
Roadside rest areas are for fatigue management and can have signed time limits. Councils may enforce separate overnight parking rules.

sections.heading: Fire and alpine access
body: Victoria's fire danger can escalate quickly. Check VicEmergency and park alerts, and never light a fire when restrictions prohibit it.
Alpine and forest roads close seasonally or after storms. Respect gates and carry a lower-altitude alternative.

sections.heading: Parks Victoria and the booking system
body: Victorian national park camping is booked through Parks Victoria, with fees varying by site category. Popular coastal sites along the Great Ocean Road and in Wilsons Promontory book out months ahead and run ballots for peak periods.
Wilsons Promontory in particular allocates summer sites by ballot rather than first booking, which catches out travellers expecting to reserve normally. Check the process well before your dates.
Many sites have vehicle and occupancy limits stated on the booking. Bring what you booked for, because sites are compact and rangers do check at busy grounds.
tips: Wilsons Prom runs a summer ballot

sections.heading: State forests and dispersed camping
body: Victoria has extensive state forest where dispersed camping is permitted free of charge, subject to fire restrictions and seasonal road closures. This is where most of the state's genuinely free camping happens.
Camp on existing cleared sites rather than creating new ones, stay away from waterways and roads by the stated minimum distances, and take all rubbish out. There are no facilities.
Seasonal road closures in the High Country and other forest areas typically run from June to November, protecting tracks that are fragile when wet. Driving a closed road carries substantial fines.

sections.heading: Fire restrictions and the danger period
body: Victoria's declared fire danger period varies by region and usually covers summer into autumn. During it, campfires are restricted and on total fire ban days all open flame including solid fuel barbecues is prohibited.

Fires must be in a properly constructed fireplace, no larger than one metre by one metre, with a three metre clear space and someone in attendance at all times. These conditions apply even outside a ban.
Check the CFA fire danger rating for your district each morning in summer. Campgrounds in forest are among the worst places to shelter on a bad day, and leaving early is the standard advice.
tips: One metre fire, three metre clearance

sections.heading: Free camping and the coast
body: Coastal councils along the Great Ocean Road and the Mornington Peninsula prohibit overnight vehicle camping almost entirely and enforce it actively. Assume prohibited unless signage says otherwise.
Inland, several councils provide free or low-cost camping in towns to attract travellers, and Victorian showgrounds frequently offer cheap sites with power and amenities.
Rest areas managed by the state road authority are for fatigue breaks. A sleep is fine; setting up camp is not, and the distinction matters where enforcement is active.
tips: Rest areas are for sleep, not camp

sections.heading: Alpine and river camping specifics
body: Camping in Victorian alpine areas is restricted above certain elevations to protect fragile vegetation, and specific distances from water and roads apply in state forest.
River frontage camping on Crown land requires awareness of licensed water frontages, some of which permit camping and some of which do not. Signage and the state's public land maps are the guide.
Parks Victoria publishes seasonal road closure dates each year, and checking them before planning a High Country route saves a wasted drive to a locked gate.
Total fire ban days prohibit solid fuel entirely, so carrying a gas cooker means the trip never depends on being allowed to light a fire.

camping-rules-tasmania.title: Camping rules in Tasmania
camping-rules-tasmania.description: Park passes, booked campgrounds, changing weather and low-impact camps in Tasmania.
camping-rules-tasmania.intro: Tasmania combines small free camps, national park sites and commercial holiday parks. Weather and sensitive environments make the details of each site important.

sections.heading: Parks passes and bookings
body: A valid parks pass is required when entering Tasmania's national parks. Camping fees or bookings can be separate from park entry.
Freycinet and other popular areas can use seasonal booking or ballot arrangements. Check before building fixed ferry and driving dates around one campground.

sections.heading: Free camps and local rules
body: Council and community camps can have registration, donation, vehicle-type or maximum-stay rules. Read signs and do not assume an old review still reflects the current arrangement.
Keep wastewater contained and use public dump points. Camp only on durable ground outside exclusion zones.

sections.heading: Weather and biosecurity
body: Tasmanian weather changes fast. Pack for cold rain in summer and avoid exposed camps when severe wind is forecast.
Clean boots, bikes and camping gear to avoid moving soil, seeds and aquatic pests between sensitive places.

sections.heading: Parks passes are compulsory
body: A Tasmania Parks Pass is required for vehicle entry to all national parks, and it is separate from any camping fee. A holiday pass covering all parks for eight weeks is far better value than daily passes if you visit more than two.
Passes are checked at major parks including Cradle Mountain and Freycinet, and fines apply for entering without one. Buy online before you travel rather than at the gate.
Cradle Mountain also runs a mandatory shuttle from the visitor centre during the day, with private vehicle access restricted. Factor the shuttle timetable into your plans.
tips: Parks pass required for vehicle entry

sections.heading: Quarantine at the border
body: Tasmania enforces strict biosecurity on arrival by ferry or air. Fresh fruit and vegetables, plants, soil, honey and used beekeeping equipment are all restricted, and detector dogs work the ferry terminal.
Clean camping gear, boots and bicycles before travelling, and dispose of fresh produce before boarding rather than having it confiscated. Fines apply for undeclared items.
The rules exist because Tasmania is free of several pests and diseases present on the mainland. Complying takes a few minutes and protects an island agricultural economy.
tips: No fresh produce across Bass Strait
Clean boots and gear before travel

sections.heading: Alpine weather in any season
body: Tasmania's weather is the most changeable in Australia and highland areas can get snow in any month. Walks above the treeline are alpine outings regardless of the date or the forecast at the car park.
Carry warm and waterproof layers on every walk, including in January. Hypothermia is the most common serious problem on Tasmanian day walks and it develops quickly in wind and rain.
Register your intentions in the log books at track heads. They are the first thing checked when someone is overdue and they have shortened searches repeatedly.
tips: Fill in track head log books

sections.heading: Free camping and the west
body: Tasmania has a good network of free and low-cost council camping areas, many in small towns, and the state is compact enough that you are rarely far from one. Stay limits are typically 24 to 72 hours.
National park campgrounds range from basic to serviced and are booked or first come depending on the site. Freycinet and Cradle Mountain both require booking in the peak season.
The west coast is wet, remote and sparsely serviced. Fill fuel at Queenstown or Strahan and carry supplies, because the gaps between towns on that side of the island are meaningful.
tips: Good network of free council sites
Book Freycinet and Cradle in season
Fuel up before the west coast

sections.heading: Walking track regulations
body: The Overland Track requires a booking and fee in the walking season with a one-way north to south direction. Other multi-day walks have their own permit and registration requirements.
Fuel stove only areas apply across much of the Tasmanian wilderness, prohibiting campfires entirely regardless of the fire danger rating. Carry a stove and check the status for your route.
Tasmania's compact size means you are rarely more than an hour from a town, which makes resupply straightforward compared with mainland remote travel.
Fuel stove only areas cover much of the Tasmanian wilderness and apply regardless of the fire danger rating, so check the status for your specific route.
tips: Fuel stove only areas are common

camping-rules-south-australia.title: Camping rules in South Australia
camping-rules-south-australia.description: Book campsites, understand fire restrictions and camp responsibly in South Australian parks.
camping-rules-south-australia.intro: South Australian national park camping is generally booked before arrival. Vehicle entry, campsite fees and fire rules can be separate parts of the same stay.

sections.heading: Book before you go
body: Reserve the campsite online or through an authorised booking agent. Check the permitted vehicle number, site dimensions and check-in details before paying.
Keep the confirmation on your phone. Park entry can be restricted for safety, conservation or operational reasons even after a booking is made.

sections.heading: Campfires and pets
body: Check the park page, Country Fire Service restrictions and park alerts before using any flame. Bring clean firewood only where allowed and use supplied fire pits.
Most national parks do not allow pets. A lead does not override a no-pet rule.

sections.heading: Remote country
body: Outback tracks and camps can close after rain. Contact the park or local authority when conditions are uncertain, and do not damage a road by pushing through.
Carry water, fuel and an emergency communication plan appropriate to the distance.

sections.heading: Parks passes and booking
body: South Australian national park camping is booked online and many parks charge vehicle entry as well as camping. A multi-park or annual pass is available and worth it if you are visiting several.
Some parks, including the Flinders Ranges and Innamincka, have desert parks passes or specific permits. Check what your route needs before setting out, because gates and rangers do check.
Sites in popular parks fill over school holidays and long weekends, particularly in the Flinders and along the coast. Outside those, availability is generally good a few days ahead.
tips: Vehicle entry often separate from camping

sections.heading: Fruit fly quarantine
body: South Australia maintains fruit fly exclusion zones and prohibits bringing fresh fruit and some vegetables across its borders and into the Riverland. Quarantine bins are provided at road borders and checkpoints operate.
Fines apply regardless of whether you knew, so plan your shopping around it: buy fresh produce after the border rather than before. This catches out a large number of travellers each year.
There are also internal checkpoints entering the Riverland zone. Carrying produce within the state can be an offence even after a legal purchase elsewhere in South Australia.
tips: No fresh produce across the border

sections.heading: Outback travel and permits
body: Travel on the Oodnadatta, Strzelecki and Birdsville tracks and into the far north requires genuine preparation, and some routes cross Aboriginal land requiring permits arranged in advance.
The Desert Parks Pass covers entry and camping in several remote parks and includes route information. It is required rather than optional for parks it covers.
Carry substantial water, fuel range, recovery equipment and a satellite communication device. Roads close after rain and stay closed for days, and there is no mobile coverage.
tips: Some routes need land access permits
Roads close for days after rain

sections.heading: Fire restrictions
body: South Australia declares fire danger seasons by district, generally running from November to April. During the season, campfires are restricted and total fire bans prohibit all open flame including solid fuel barbecues.
Gas appliances are generally permitted on ban days subject to conditions including a cleared area and someone in attendance. Check the specific ban rather than assuming.
Many parks prohibit fires permanently, particularly in the arid zone where firewood collection damages fragile habitat. Bring a gas cooker and do not rely on being able to have a fire.
tips: Fire danger season November to April
Gas usually allowed on ban days
Arid parks often ban fires always

sections.heading: Coastal and conservation park rules
body: Many South Australian conservation parks permit camping only in designated areas with a booked site, and several coastal parks restrict vehicle access to protect dune systems.

Beach driving is permitted in some areas with a permit, notably along parts of the Coorong and Yorke Peninsula. Check the specific area, because driving on a closed beach carries fines and does real damage.
South Australia's parks system publishes campground alerts for fire risk and track closures, and these change quickly in summer across the arid parks.
Desert parks require their own pass covering entry and camping, and it is a requirement rather than an optional convenience for the parks it covers.
tips: Designated sites only in most parks

camping-rules-western-australia.title: Camping rules in Western Australia
camping-rules-western-australia.description: National park bookings, entry fees and long-distance camping across Western Australia.
camping-rules-western-australia.intro: Western Australian camping rules vary across national parks, local government land, pastoral areas and private parks. Large distances make a closed or full campground more than a minor inconvenience.

sections.heading: Park Stay WA and fees
body: Many national park camps are booked through Park Stay WA. Camping fees are usually charged per person per night, and park entry can be separate.
Some campgrounds remain first come, first served. Arrive early and keep a legal alternative within your fuel range.

sections.heading: Roadside and remote camping
body: Use signed overnight areas and keep heavy-vehicle bays free. Local governments can prohibit camping outside licensed grounds, including beaches and town parking areas.
On remote roads, check access, station permission and Aboriginal land permit requirements before leaving the highway.

sections.heading: Fire, water and distance
body: Carry drinking water and verify whether campground taps are potable. Fire restrictions differ by district and season.
Do not collect firewood in protected areas. Heat and wind can make a legal morning fire unsafe or prohibited by afternoon.

sections.heading: The scale changes the planning
body: Western Australia covers a third of the continent and the distances between parks, towns and fuel are unlike anywhere else. A camping trip here is a logistics exercise before it is anything else.
Parks and Wildlife campgrounds are booked online for popular sites and first come for many remote ones. A parks pass covering vehicle entry is available and is worth it beyond a few visits.
Many northern parks close for the wet season, roughly November to April, and reopen when roads and crossings allow. Check the current status rather than the published season.
tips: Northern parks close in the wet

sections.heading: Free camping and the 24 hour rule
body: Many WA local governments permit 24 hour stays in designated rest areas and prohibit camping elsewhere. Shire rules vary widely, and the more remote the shire, the more relaxed it generally is.

Some rest areas along the North West Coastal Highway and the Great Northern Highway allow longer stays and are effectively free campgrounds. Signage states the limit and it is enforced in busier areas.

Station stays, where pastoral properties open camping areas to travellers, are a distinctive WA option and often the only accommodation for hundreds of kilometres. Most take cash and few have reliable booking.

sections.heading: Water, fuel and communication
body: Carry a minimum of four to five litres of drinking water per person per day plus a substantial reserve, and treat fuel range as the constraint that shapes the route. Roadhouses can be closed, out of fuel or card-only with unreliable connections.
Mobile coverage exists near towns and disappears entirely between them. A satellite messenger or personal locator beacon is standard equipment for remote WA travel rather than an optional extra.
Tell someone your route and expected arrival. If you break down, stay with the vehicle, which is shelter and is far easier to find than a person walking.
tips: Five litres per person per day

sections.heading: Heat, cyclones and the dry
body: The dry season from May to October is when the north works. The wet brings extreme humidity, monsoonal rain, cyclones between November and April, and widespread closures.
In the south west, the pattern reverses: winter is wet and cool, summer is hot and dry, and spring brings the wildflowers. The two halves of the state need completely different planning.
Heat is the underrated risk. Inland summer temperatures regularly exceed forty degrees, and vehicle breakdown in that heat without adequate water is genuinely life threatening.
tips: Inland heat is a genuine risk

sections.heading: Aboriginal land and access permits
body: Substantial areas of Western Australia are Aboriginal land requiring an entry permit, including sections of routes through the Kimberley and the interior. Permits are applied for in advance through the relevant body.
Some routes require a transit permit even if you are not stopping. Check whether your intended road crosses land requiring one, because they are not issued at the boundary.
Western Australia's parks agency publishes campground availability and closures online, which matters because the distances mean a closed site can cost a full day.
Distances between parks in Western Australia mean a closed campground can cost a full day, so confirm availability before committing to a long drive.
tips: Permits apply in advance, not at the gate
Check the route, not just the destination

camping-rules-northern-territory.title: Camping rules in the Northern Territory
camping-rules-northern-territory.description: Online campsite bookings, visitor passes and remote permits in NT parks.
camping-rules-northern-territory.intro: Designated NT park campsites generally require online booking and payment before arrival. Visitor passes and special permits can apply as well.

sections.heading: Bookings and visitor passes
body: Book designated campsites through the NT parks system and keep the camping tag available. Rangers cannot always accept payment at the campground.
Visitors need an NT Parks Visitor Pass for most participating parks and reserves. Kakadu uses separate national park arrangements.

sections.heading: Camping outside designated areas
body: A permit is required to camp overnight outside designated areas and for specific protected places such as Garig Gunak Barlu. Apply with enough time for assessment.
Remote permission does not remove the need for route, water, heat and communication planning.

sections.heading: Seasonal access and water safety
body: Wet-season flooding closes roads and campgrounds. Check the latest park page even when the weather is dry where you are standing.
Follow crocodile and swimming signs at every waterbody. Conditions and permitted swimming areas change.

sections.heading: Permits for Aboriginal land
body: Large areas of the Territory are Aboriginal freehold land requiring a permit to enter or transit, including much of Arnhem Land and sections of major routes. Permits are applied for through the relevant land council in advance.

Permits take time to process and are not issued at the boundary. Plan several weeks ahead for Arnhem Land, and check whether your route crosses land requiring a transit permit even if you are not stopping.
Alcohol restrictions apply across many Territory communities and areas, with substantial penalties for carrying alcohol into restricted zones. Check before travelling with any in the vehicle.
tips: Transit permits apply to some routes

sections.heading: Kakadu, Litchfield and park passes
body: Kakadu requires a park pass purchased in advance, while Litchfield does not. Uluru-Kata Tjuta and Watarrka have their own arrangements, so check each park rather than assuming a single Territory system.

Many of the best sites in Kakadu require high clearance four-wheel drive and involve creek crossings, which most standard hire agreements prohibit. Litchfield delivers more per day for a two-wheel drive.
Sacred sites within parks have photography and access restrictions marked by signage. These are conditions of access rather than suggestions, and respecting them matters.
tips: Kakadu needs a pass, Litchfield does not
Jim Jim and Twin Falls need 4WD

sections.heading: Crocodiles and water
body: Estuarine crocodiles are present throughout the Top End in rivers, creeks, billabongs, estuaries and along the coast. Any waterway should be assumed to contain them unless a current sign says otherwise.
Swimming holes are surveyed and opened seasonally, and the status changes. Check on the day rather than relying on a previous visit or a guidebook, and never camp at the water's edge.
Freshwater crocodiles are also widespread and generally leave people alone, but telling the two apart from a distance is not a reliable skill. Treat all crocodile habitat the same way.
tips: Never camp at the water's edge

sections.heading: The build-up and the seasons
body: The Territory runs on two seasons plus the build-up. The dry, from May to September, is comfortable and busy. The build-up in October and November brings extreme humidity before the rain arrives.
The wet, from December to March, brings monsoonal rain, road closures, and closure of many parks and campgrounds. It also brings the waterfalls to full flow, which some travellers prefer.
Central Australia is different again: hot summers exceeding forty degrees and cold winter nights below freezing. Pack for a large diurnal swing rather than a single temperature.

sections.heading: Fishing, hunting and collecting
body: Recreational fishing in the Territory has size and bag limits and some areas are closed. Barramundi in particular have seasonal closures, and the rules differ between tidal and fresh water.
Collecting firewood, plants, rocks and artefacts is prohibited in parks and reserves. Artefacts in particular are protected and removing them is a serious offence.
Territory parks publish seasonal opening dates that shift with the wet, so confirm a campground is open rather than relying on the published season.
Alcohol restrictions apply across many Territory regions with substantial penalties, so check before travelling with any in the vehicle.
tips: Artefact removal is a serious offence

camping-rules-act.title: Camping rules in the ACT
camping-rules-act.description: Approved campgrounds, protected areas, fires and closures around Canberra.
camping-rules-act.intro: Camping in the ACT is limited to approved campgrounds and their conditions. Namadgi, Cotter and other areas can close during fire danger or severe weather.

sections.heading: Choose an approved campground
body: Use territory or privately managed campgrounds where overnight stays are expressly allowed. Picnic areas, trailheads and suburban parking spaces are not substitutes.
Check bookings, gate hours, vehicle size, generators and pet rules for the exact campground.

sections.heading: Namadgi and remote walks
body: Namadgi protects sensitive natural and cultural places. Camp only in permitted areas and follow track, group and fire conditions.
Leave a trip intention with someone reliable when walking beyond busy areas. Mobile coverage is uneven.

sections.heading: Fire and water
body: ACT fire danger can close parks at short notice. Check Emergency Services Agency advice and park alerts before departure.
Treat water unless the campground clearly identifies a maintained potable supply. Carry enough for the full stay when uncertain.

sections.heading: A small territory with clear rules
body: The ACT is compact and camping options are limited to Namadgi National Park, Cotter and a small number of designated areas. There is essentially no informal or roadside camping permitted anywhere in the territory.
Namadgi campgrounds are mostly free but require registration, and the park covers around half the territory's land area. Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear are the main sites.
Because the ACT is surrounded by NSW, most travellers end up camping across the border. Check which jurisdiction you are actually in, because the rules and fees differ immediately.
tips: No informal camping in the ACT
Namadgi sites are free but need registration
Rules change instantly at the NSW border

sections.heading: Namadgi and the alpine conditions
body: Namadgi rises to over 1,900 metres and the higher country carries snow in winter. Conditions at Mount Clear are considerably colder than Canberra, and visitors regularly underestimate the difference.

The park was heavily burnt in the 2019 to 2020 fires and regeneration continues, with some tracks and facilities altered. Check the current status with the visitor centre before planning specific walks.
Water in the park should be treated. Tanks at campgrounds are rainwater and not guaranteed potable, and creek water carries the usual risks.
tips: Treat all water in the park

sections.heading: Fire restrictions and the danger period
body: The ACT declares a bushfire danger period, usually from October to March, during which fires are restricted. Total fire bans prohibit all open flame including solid fuel barbecues.
Namadgi prohibits campfires entirely in most areas year round, and gas cookers are the practical option. Check the current park conditions before assuming a fireplace can be used.
The territory has burnt severely twice in living memory, in 2003 and 2020. Fire danger ratings are taken seriously here and leaving early on a bad day is standard practice.
tips: Gas cooker is the practical option

sections.heading: Using Canberra as a base
body: Canberra has caravan parks close to the centre and is compact enough that day trips reach Namadgi, Tidbinbilla and the Brindabellas easily. For many travellers this works better than camping in the park.
Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve has koalas, platypus and rock wallabies in an accessible setting and charges vehicle entry. It is a good half day and considerably easier than the Namadgi walks.
The national institutions, including the War Memorial, Questacon and the National Gallery, are mostly free and make excellent wet-weather options if the mountain forecast is poor.
tips: Caravan parks close to the centre
Tidbinbilla is an accessible half day
Free national institutions for wet days

sections.heading: Cotter and the reserves
body: The Cotter Reserve and Casuarina Sands offer day use and limited camping close to Canberra, and they are heavily used on summer weekends. Alcohol restrictions apply at several of these sites.
Murrumbidgee River Corridor sites permit swimming but the river has strong currents and submerged hazards. Check conditions and swim only where signage permits it.
Because the ACT is small, most travellers treat it as a stop rather than a destination, using Canberra as a base and camping across the border in New South Wales.
Namadgi is considerably colder than Canberra and carries snow in winter, so pack for mountain conditions rather than the city forecast.
tips: Cotter is busy on summer weekends
River currents are stronger than they look

is-free-camping-legal-australia.title: Is free camping legal in Australia?
is-free-camping-legal-australia.description: Free camping is legal only where the land manager allows an overnight stay.
is-free-camping-legal-australia.intro: Australia has free camps, but there is no national right to camp wherever a vehicle can park. The rule comes from the exact land, sign and local authority.

sections.heading: Parking is not camping permission
body: A legal parking space may still prohibit sleeping, setting up camp or staying overnight. Look for explicit overnight permission, time limits and vehicle restrictions.
Do not rely on the absence of a no-camping sign. Confirm the land manager or council rule when the purpose of the area is unclear.

sections.heading: Places that may be free
body: Some council camps, community reserves, national park sites and roadside areas charge no nightly fee. Registration, booking, donation or maximum-stay conditions may still apply.
Rest areas primarily manage fatigue. Keep truck spaces clear and avoid awnings, chairs or levelling setups that turn a short rest into an illegal camp.

sections.heading: Leave the place open
body: Contain rubbish and wastewater, use toilets where provided and move on within the allowed stay. Noise, fires and sprawling setups are common reasons communities restrict free camping.
If a site is full, do not invent a new bay on vegetation or a nearby street.

sections.heading: There is no national answer
body: Free camping legality is set by whoever manages the land: state parks agencies, state forests, local councils, road authorities and private owners all apply different rules. There is no Australia-wide position to learn.

The practical consequence is that the answer changes at every local government boundary, and those boundaries are invisible from the road. A rule confirmed in one shire tells you nothing about the next.
The reliable sources are the signage at the specific location and the relevant council's website. Everything else, including apps and guidebooks, is a starting point rather than an authority.
tips: Answer changes at each shire boundary

sections.heading: Where it is generally permitted
body: State forests in Victoria, NSW and Queensland permit dispersed camping free of charge in most areas, subject to fire restrictions and seasonal closures. This is the most reliable free camping in the eastern states.

Many inland councils, particularly in Queensland, NSW and South Australia, provide free or donation-based camping to attract travellers into town. These are signed, welcomed and often have basic facilities.
Station stays and roadhouse camping fill the gaps in remote areas. Both are usually inexpensive rather than free, and both are frequently the only option for hundreds of kilometres.
tips: State forests are the reliable option

sections.heading: Where it is generally prohibited
body: Coastal councils near major cities and in tourist areas almost universally prohibit overnight camping in vehicles, and enforce it with patrols and fines. Assume prohibited on any popular coastline unless signage says otherwise.
National parks require a permit and a designated campground almost everywhere. Camping outside designated areas in a national park is an offence in every state.

Rest areas managed by road authorities are for fatigue breaks. Sleeping is generally fine; setting up camp with awnings and chairs is not what they are provided for and is often explicitly prohibited.
tips: Rest areas are for fatigue only

sections.heading: Self-containment and behaviour
body: Some councils permit free camping only for self-contained vehicles with onboard toilet and waste storage. The definition varies between councils and some require certification while others rely on a declaration.
Regardless of the rules, behaviour is what keeps sites open. Arrive late, leave early, keep the footprint small, take all rubbish, and never empty waste anywhere but a dump point.
Sites close because of waste, noise and overcrowding, and closures are usually permanent. The districts with the strictest rules today are the ones where behaviour was worst previously.

sections.heading: Tools that actually help
body: Council websites, state parks pages and the signage itself are the authoritative sources. Camping apps and community listings are useful for finding candidates and are not a defence if a site turns out to be prohibited.
Where a listing and a sign disagree, follow the sign and report the discrepancy so the listing improves. Enforcement officers work from the local law and the sign, not from any app.
When in genuine doubt, a low-cost council site or a showground is usually within reach and removes the question entirely for a very small amount of money.
Photographing the sign when you arrive costs nothing and is the only evidence that reliably helps if an infringement is later disputed.
tips: Officers work from the local law

campfires-camping-australia.title: Campfire rules for camping in Australia
campfires-camping-australia.description: Check local fire bans, park rules and weather before striking a match.
campfires-camping-australia.imageAlt: Legal campfire in a designated fire ring
campfires-camping-australia.intro: Campfire permission can change with the district, season, fuel type and fire danger rating. A fire ring proves that fires have been used there, not that one is legal today.

sections.heading: Three checks before lighting
body: Read the campground rules, check the relevant state fire authority and look for local park alerts. Complete fire bans override normal campground permission.
Gas cookers can also be restricted during severe conditions. Check the rule for the appliance, not only open fires.

sections.heading: Firewood and setup
body: Collecting timber is prohibited in many parks because fallen wood is habitat. Bring clean, untreated firewood only where the land manager allows it.
Use an existing fireplace, clear the immediate area as directed and keep water beside you. Never light beneath branches or in strong wind.

sections.heading: Put it out cold
body: Extinguish with water, stir the remains and repeat until everything is cold enough to touch. Sand can hide hot embers rather than extinguish them.
Never leave a fire unattended, including while sleeping. If wind rises or conditions feel wrong, put it out.

sections.heading: Fire danger ratings and total fire bans
body: Australia uses a national Fire Danger Rating system with four levels from Moderate to Catastrophic, published daily by district. Total fire bans are declared separately and prohibit all open flame regardless of the rating.

On a total fire ban day, campfires and solid fuel barbecues are prohibited. Gas appliances are generally permitted with conditions including a cleared area and constant attendance, but the specific ban wording governs.
Ratings and bans are published each afternoon for the following day. Check them daily in summer rather than relying on how the weather feels, because the declaration is based on forecast conditions.
tips: Four rating levels, Moderate to Catastrophic

sections.heading: Where fires are permitted at all
body: Many national parks prohibit campfires permanently, particularly in arid zones where firewood collection destroys habitat that takes decades to form. Others permit them only in provided fireplaces.
Collecting firewood is prohibited in most national parks and reserves. Bring your own from outside the area, and be aware that some regions also restrict moving firewood to limit pest spread.
Check the specific campground page rather than the state-wide position. The land manager's rule is stricter than the fire danger system in many places and applies year round.

sections.heading: Building and controlling a legal fire
body: Where permitted, use an existing fireplace, keep the fire small, clear combustible material well back and have water immediately beside you rather than in the vehicle. Never light in wind or under overhanging branches.

Typical legal conditions specify a maximum fire size, a cleared radius of several metres and constant adult attendance. These apply outside total fire bans as well, and breaching them carries penalties.
Never leave a fire unattended, including while it burns down. Most escaped campfires start after the people who lit them decided it was nearly out.
tips: Water beside you, not in the vehicle

sections.heading: Putting it out and the consequences
body: A fire is out when it is cold to the touch. Douse it, stir the ashes, douse again and keep going until you can put your hand in the remains. Embers survive under ash for many hours.

Escaped fires carry severe penalties in every state, including large fines and imprisonment where negligence is established. You can also be liable for suppression costs, which run into very large sums.
If a fire escapes, do not attempt to fight it beyond the first seconds. Move away and call triple zero immediately with the clearest location you can give.
tips: Out means cold to the touch

sections.heading: Cooking when fires are banned
body: Gas cookers are generally permitted on total fire ban days subject to conditions: a cleared area, a person in attendance and immediate access to water. Check the specific ban wording, because conditions vary by state.

Never cook inside a tent, an awning or an unventilated vehicle. Carbon monoxide is odourless and has killed campers, and the risk is highest in exactly the cold or wet conditions that tempt people indoors.
Keep a lightweight gas cooker in the vehicle permanently, because a total fire ban can be declared with a day's notice and it removes any dependence on lighting a fire.
Fire danger ratings are published each afternoon for the following day, so checking them the evening before gives you time to change plans rather than react.
tips: Never cook in a closed space

sleeping-in-car-australia.title: Can you sleep in your car in Australia?
sleeping-in-car-australia.description: Sleeping in a car is allowed only where local land, parking and vehicle rules permit it.
sleeping-in-car-australia.imageAlt: Campervan parked at an authorised overnight site
sleeping-in-car-australia.intro: The vehicle does not make the location legal. Council bylaws, signs, park rules and private property rights decide whether you can sleep there.

sections.heading: Read the location, not the internet
body: Check signs for parking hours, no-camping rules and vehicle restrictions. Beach carparks and residential streets are commonly monitored in busy visitor towns.
An old review does not protect you from a fine. Use the current council or land-manager information.

sections.heading: Rest areas
body: Driver-reviver and highway rest areas exist to reduce fatigue. Some allow a limited overnight rest, while others prohibit camping or restrict vehicle types.
Keep truck bays free, contain noise and do not spread equipment outside the vehicle unless the area permits camping.

sections.heading: Safer alternatives
body: A basic campground, showground, caravan park or farm stay provides clearer permission and often toilets or water. Arrive before dark and confirm access for the vehicle.
Never sleep with a fuel-burning heater or cooker operating inside a closed vehicle.

sections.heading: Parking legally is not the same as camping legally
body: A vehicle can be lawfully parked somewhere and still be prohibited from being slept in. That distinction is what most infringements turn on, and it is why travellers who checked the parking signs still get fined.

Council local laws govern this and they vary at every boundary. Some permit sleeping in a vehicle in designated areas, many prohibit it in all public places, and enforcement is heaviest in coastal and tourist areas.
Read the signage for the specific bay, not the street. Time-limited parking, permit zones and overnight prohibitions are frequently signed separately and all apply at once.
tips: Parking legally does not permit sleeping
Rules change at every council boundary
Read the sign for the specific bay

sections.heading: Where it is generally accepted
body: Designated rest areas along highways permit sleeping for fatigue management, usually up to 24 hours, and this is the most reliably legal option nationwide. They are for rest rather than for setting up camp.
Many inland council towns provide free or low-cost overnight areas that expressly permit sleeping in vehicles. Showgrounds and sports grounds often do the same for a small fee.
Some 24 hour service stations and roadhouses permit overnight parking, particularly on long highway routes. Ask inside rather than assuming, and buy something.
tips: Rest areas allow up to 24 hours
Ask at roadhouses rather than assume

sections.heading: Doing it safely
body: Choose somewhere with other vehicles present, lighting and an easy exit. Park facing out where you can, keep valuables out of sight, and lock the doors while keeping a clear way to get out quickly.

Ventilation matters more than people expect. A sealed car with people sleeping in it gets humid and stuffy quickly, and in heat it becomes genuinely dangerous. Crack windows with insect screens if you have them.
Never run the engine for air conditioning while sleeping. Exhaust can enter the cabin, and carbon monoxide is odourless and has killed people doing exactly this.
tips: Park facing out, keep an exit clear
Ventilate, do not seal the car
Never idle the engine while sleeping

sections.heading: Heat, cold and the practical limits
body: An Australian summer makes sleeping in an unventilated car unsafe rather than uncomfortable. Interior temperatures rise fast and stay high overnight in the north, and this is the leading practical reason not to do it.
In winter, inland and alpine nights drop below freezing and a car offers almost no insulation. A proper sleeping bag rated to the conditions matters more in a vehicle than in a tent.
If you are doing this regularly, a window shade set, insect screens and a decent mattress transform it. Without those it works for a night and becomes miserable across a week.
tips: Cars overheat overnight in the north

sections.heading: Making a car workable for a night
body: Window shades, insect screens and a proper mattress transform sleeping in a car from an endurance exercise into something repeatable. Without them it works for one night and becomes miserable across a week.
Level ground matters more than it sounds, and a slight slope that is unnoticeable when parked becomes obvious once lying down. Turning the vehicle around is often enough to fix it.
For longer trips, a small van or a wagon with the seats folded gives far more usable room than a sedan for very little extra hire cost.
Australian summer heat makes an unventilated car genuinely unsafe overnight, which is the practical limit on this approach rather than any local law.
tips: Level ground matters when lying down
Turning around often fixes a slope

driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.title: Driving in Australia with an overseas licence
driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.description: Licence rules differ between states and territories, especially for longer stays.
driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.imageAlt: Campervan driving on an Australian road
driving-in-australia-overseas-licence.intro: International visitors can often drive on a current overseas licence for a limited period, but each state and territory sets its own conditions.

sections.heading: Check every jurisdiction
body: Confirm the rule with the transport authority for each state or territory on the route. Residency, visa status and length of stay can change what is required.
Carry the original licence. If it is not in English, bring an accepted English translation or International Driving Permit as required.

sections.heading: Vehicle class and rental terms
body: Your licence must cover the vehicle class and weight. A motorhome can be larger than the passenger vehicle you normally drive.
Rental agreements can prohibit unsealed roads, beaches, floodwater and driving after dark. Insurance may not cover a breach.

sections.heading: Australian road habits
body: Drive on the left, learn local roundabout rules and leave more braking distance in a heavy vehicle. Long rural distances make fatigue a major risk.
Stop before tiredness becomes obvious. Avoid dawn and dusk on wildlife-heavy roads.

sections.heading: Rental company conditions sit on top of the law
body: Even where the law permits you to drive, rental companies apply their own rules: a minimum age, a licence held for a minimum period, young driver surcharges and sometimes refusal of licences from particular countries.
Confirm these at booking rather than at the counter. Being refused a vehicle at an airport depot after a long flight is a genuinely difficult problem to solve.
Many agreements also prohibit specific roads, unsealed surfaces and beach driving entirely, with damage on them uninsured. Read those clauses before planning a route.

sections.heading: Translations and international permits
body: A licence not in English needs an accurate English translation or an International Driving Permit, carried alongside the original. The permit supports the licence rather than replacing it, so both must be present.
Get the permit in your home country before travelling, because it generally cannot be issued once you have arrived. It is inexpensive and quick to obtain from the relevant motoring authority.
Carry both documents in the vehicle at all times. Police can require them at a roadside stop and being unable to produce them is an offence in its own right.
tips: IDP supports, never replaces, the licence
Obtain the IDP before you travel

sections.heading: Vehicle class and campervans
body: A standard car licence in most Australian states covers vehicles up to 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass and twelve occupants including the driver. Larger motorhomes require a light rigid or medium rigid class.
Your home licence class determines the Australian equivalence, and a car licence in one country does not automatically cover a 4.5 tonne vehicle. Check before booking a large motorhome.
Towing adds further constraints. The combination weight, not just the vehicle, determines what class you need, and exceeding it affects insurance as well as legality.
tips: Large motorhomes may need a higher class
Towing is assessed on combination weight

sections.heading: Insurance and what excess reduction covers
body: Rental excess amounts in Australia are typically high, frequently several thousand dollars. Excess reduction products lower it but commonly exclude windscreens, tyres, undercarriage, water damage and single-vehicle accidents.

Those exclusions cover most of what actually happens on Australian roads, particularly on gravel. Read what is excluded rather than what is covered, and price a separate policy if the exclusions matter.

Third party injury cover works differently from many countries and varies by state. Compulsory third party insurance is included with registration, but property damage to others is not automatically covered.
tips: Excess is often several thousand dollars
Glass and tyres are usually excluded

sections.heading: Roadside assistance and breakdowns
body: Check whether roadside assistance is included with your rental and what it covers in remote areas, because many policies limit towing distance and remote recovery is extremely expensive.

Carry the assistance number written down as well as in a phone, and be able to describe your location using the nearest roadside marker or landmark. In remote areas, staying with the vehicle is always the right decision.
Take photographs of your licence, permit and rental agreement and store them separately, so a lost wallet does not also end the driving part of the trip.
Rental agreements commonly exclude unsealed roads entirely, so confirm what your vehicle is permitted to drive on before planning a route through gravel country.

interstate-biosecurity-road-trip.title: Interstate biosecurity for Australian road trips
interstate-biosecurity-road-trip.description: Fruit, vegetables, honey, plants, soil and camping gear can be restricted at state borders.
interstate-biosecurity-road-trip.intro: Australia has quarantine zones within the country. Carrying the wrong produce or dirty equipment can spread pests and lead to an on-the-spot fine.

sections.heading: Check before shopping
body: Rules vary by product, origin and destination. Check the official traveller information before crossing a state or quarantine-zone border.
Fresh fruit, vegetables, honey, plants and soil are common concerns. Restrictions can apply even when the item was bought in an Australian supermarket.

sections.heading: Use quarantine bins
body: Eat allowed produce before the border or place restricted items in a quarantine bin. Do not hide food in the vehicle or leave it beside the road.
Keep receipts and packaging when official advice says a commercially treated product is permitted.

sections.heading: Clean camping equipment
body: Remove soil, seeds and plant material from boots, tents, bikes and recovery gear. Dry water equipment before moving between catchments where required.
Clean gear also lasts longer and avoids carrying ants, weeds and pathogens into the next campground.

sections.heading: Fruit fly zones are the main issue
body: South Australia, Tasmania and parts of Victoria and New South Wales maintain fruit fly exclusion zones. Carrying fresh fruit and some vegetables into them is prohibited, with disposal bins provided at borders and checkpoints operating.
Fines apply whether or not you knew, and inspections at the South Australian border and the Tasmanian ferry terminal are routine. Detector dogs work some crossings.
The practical approach is to plan shopping around the borders: run the fridge down before a crossing and restock immediately after. This costs nothing and removes the problem entirely.
tips: Run the fridge down before a border

sections.heading: Tasmania and Western Australia
body: Tasmania restricts fresh produce, plants, soil, honey and used beekeeping equipment on arrival by ferry or air. The rules protect an island free of several mainland pests and are enforced at the terminal.

Western Australia operates quarantine checkpoints on eastern approaches including the Eyre Highway, restricting fruit, vegetables, honey, plants and soil. This catches travellers who stocked up before crossing the Nullarbor.
Both jurisdictions publish current restricted item lists that change with outbreaks. Check before travelling rather than relying on what applied on a previous trip.
tips: Tasmania checks at the ferry terminal
WA checkpoints on the Eyre Highway

sections.heading: Soil, gear and weeds
body: Soil on boots, tent pegs, bicycles and vehicles moves plant pathogens and weed seeds between regions. Phytophthora dieback in Western Australia is spread this way and has devastated large areas of native vegetation.
Clean footwear and gear between regions, use the cleaning stations provided at park entrances in dieback areas, and stay on formed tracks and roads where signage asks you to.
Firewood also moves pests. Several regions restrict moving firewood, and buying local rather than carrying a load across state lines is the safer practice.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Australia's agricultural industries are free of many pests present elsewhere, and that status depends on internal barriers as much as international ones. A single fruit fly outbreak can cost a region's growers their export markets.
For native ecosystems the stakes are similar. Dieback, myrtle rust and weed incursions have permanently altered large areas, and most of that movement was human-assisted and avoidable.
Complying costs a few minutes and some planning around shopping. Treat the bins at a border as a normal part of a road trip rather than an inconvenience.
tips: One outbreak can close export markets

sections.heading: Planning the fridge around borders
body: Run fresh produce down in the days before a quarantine crossing and restock immediately after. This costs nothing, avoids buying food twice and removes the risk of a fine entirely.

Cooked and processed food is generally fine, so a meal plan built around tinned, dried and cooked items across a border day works well. Check the current restricted list rather than guessing which items count.
Quarantine bins at borders are provided precisely so you can comply without penalty, and using one is treated very differently from being found with undeclared produce.
Restricted item lists change with outbreaks, so check the current position rather than relying on what applied on a previous trip.
tips: Run the fridge down before crossing
Cooked and processed food is usually fine

camping-with-dogs-australia.title: Camping with dogs in Australia
camping-with-dogs-australia.description: Find dog-friendly stays without assuming pets are welcome in parks or shared campgrounds.
camping-with-dogs-australia.imageAlt: Dog resting beside a tent at a pet-friendly campground
camping-with-dogs-australia.intro: A dog-friendly road trip needs a route built around permitted camps, safe exercise, heat and wildlife. National parks commonly prohibit pets.

sections.heading: Choose the right land
body: Check the exact campground rule and any lead requirement. A listing marked dog-friendly may still exclude pets from cabins, beaches, trails or peak periods.
Never take a dog into a prohibited national park, even if it remains inside the vehicle.

sections.heading: Heat and travel
body: A parked vehicle becomes dangerous quickly. Plan walks for cool hours, carry more water than usual and choose shade before arrival.
Secure the dog safely while driving and build rest breaks around places where exercise is allowed.

sections.heading: Wildlife and other campers
body: Keep the dog controlled around kangaroos, livestock, snakes and ground-nesting birds. Do not allow barking or roaming to disturb neighbouring sites.
Collect waste every time, including in remote areas. Ask before approaching another camper or dog.

sections.heading: National parks generally exclude dogs
body: Dogs are prohibited in almost all Australian national parks, in every state, because of the risk to native wildlife and because many parks use 1080 baiting. This is the single biggest constraint on camping with a dog here.
State forests, regional parks, council reserves and private campgrounds are the workable alternatives, and many permit dogs on lead. Some state forests allow dogs off lead outside baiting periods.
Plan the route around dog-friendly places first rather than hoping to improvise. A standard national park itinerary with a dog produces a trip where somebody waits in the vehicle constantly.
tips: Dogs banned in almost all national parks
State forests are the usual alternative
Plan the route around dog-friendly stops

sections.heading: 1080 baiting is the serious risk
body: Sodium fluoroacetate, known as 1080, is used widely for fox, wild dog and rabbit control and is lethal to dogs in tiny quantities. Poisoning can occur from eating bait or from scavenging a poisoned carcass months later.
Baited areas are signed at access points and operations are published in advance by state agencies. Check before entering any state forest, reserve or pastoral area with a dog.
There is no reliable field antidote and death is distressing and rapid. Keep dogs leashed and muzzled in baited areas, or better, avoid those areas entirely.
tips: Risk persists in carcasses for months

sections.heading: Heat and vehicles
body: Heat in a parked vehicle kills dogs quickly, and shade moves through the day. An Australian summer makes leaving a dog in a vehicle unsafe even briefly, which rules out most attractions that exclude dogs.
Hot ground burns paws. Bitumen and sand reach temperatures that cause serious burns, and the test is whether you can hold the back of your hand on the surface for several seconds.
Carry more water for the dog than you think you need and offer it frequently. Dogs dehydrate faster than people in this climate and show it later.
tips: Never leave a dog in a parked vehicle
Test ground temperature with your hand
Carry extra water for the dog

sections.heading: Wildlife, ticks and snakes
body: Paralysis ticks along the east coast are potentially fatal to dogs and preventatives are essential rather than optional in that region. Check the dog daily, particularly around the head, neck and ears.
Snakes are a genuine risk and dogs frequently investigate them. Keep dogs on lead in bush and long grass, and know where the nearest veterinary clinic with antivenom is on remote legs.
Cane toads across the north are toxic if mouthed and cause rapid poisoning. In toad country, supervise dogs closely at night when toads are most active.
tips: Tick preventatives on the east coast
Keep dogs leashed in long grass
Cane toads are toxic if mouthed

sections.heading: Snakes, ticks and emergency vets
body: Snake bite in dogs is a genuine risk in warm months and requires immediate veterinary treatment. Know where the nearest clinic with antivenom is before heading somewhere remote, because time is the deciding factor.
Paralysis ticks on the east coast require preventatives and daily checking. In remote areas, the nearest vet may be hours away, which changes the risk calculation for taking a dog at all.
Where a national park is unavoidable, kennels and day-boarding operate in most regional towns and are usually inexpensive for a single day.
1080 baiting notices are published in advance by state agencies, and checking them before entering any forest or reserve with a dog is essential.
tips: Know the nearest vet with antivenom
Daily tick checks on the east coast

caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.title: Caravan park vs holiday park vs campground
caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.description: Choose the right mix of facilities, price and atmosphere for each night.
caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.imageAlt: Caravan park beside an Australian beach
caravan-park-vs-holiday-park.intro: The labels overlap, but the experience can be very different. Match the stay to what the trip needs that night rather than chasing one type for the whole route.

sections.heading: Caravan and holiday parks
body: Caravan parks focus on powered and unpowered sites, amenities and vehicle access. Holiday parks often add pools, playgrounds, cabins and a more resort-like feel.
Ask about site length, surface, power connection, check-in time and whether facilities are seasonal.

sections.heading: Bush campgrounds
body: National park and forest campgrounds trade services for location. Toilets may be basic, water may be untreated or absent and generators can be restricted.
Check road access and booking before driving in. A cheaper fee can cost more if the setup is unsuitable.

sections.heading: Use a mixed strategy
body: A simple bush camp followed by a powered holiday park makes laundry, charging and water refills easier. Roofed accommodation can rescue a route during severe weather.
