driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.title: Driving in Australia for the first time: essential road rules
driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.description: Drive on the left, understand speed and restraint rules, and know why licence conditions matter across state borders.
driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.imageAlt: Australian road seen from the left-hand driving position
driving-in-australia-road-rules-visitors.intro: Australia drives on the left, but safe visitor driving involves more than remembering the side of the road. Speed, alcohol, mobile devices and licence conditions all need a cautious, jurisdiction-aware approach.

sections.heading: Left-side habits
body: Take extra care after stops, at turns and when entering roundabouts, when old right-side habits can return. Keep the driver near the centre line and the passenger side near the kerb.
Set navigation, mirrors and controls before moving. If orientation feels wrong, stop legally and reset rather than correcting while driving.

sections.heading: Speed, restraints and devices
body: A posted limit is the legal maximum in good conditions, not a target. Slow for weather, visibility, wildlife, gravel and the vehicle’s size.
Every occupant needs the correct seating position and restraint. Portable-device rules and exceptions vary, so the safest practice is not to touch a phone while driving.

sections.heading: Alcohol and jurisdiction differences
body: Never present 0.05 as a universal allowance. Learner and provisional drivers can require zero BAC, while some heavy or passenger-vehicle categories have lower limits.
The Australian Road Rules are a national model, but every state and territory enacts its own law and can add differences. Read the authority for the place you are driving.

sections.heading: Roundabouts, hook turns and school zones
body: Roundabouts run clockwise and you give way to your right, signalling left as you exit. Multi-lane roundabouts require the correct entry lane, marked on the road surface.

Melbourne's central grid uses hook turns, where a right turn is made from the left lane after waiting for the signal. They are signed and unique to that city, and they catch out Australian drivers as well as visitors.
School zones drop to forty kilometres per hour at set times on school days and are enforced heavily with cameras. The signs show the times and they apply whether or not children are visible.
tips: Give way to the right on roundabouts

sections.heading: Level crossings, trams and cyclists
body: Many rural level crossings are passive, marked only with signs rather than lights or booms. Slow, look both ways and be aware that trains on regional lines are infrequent enough that people stop expecting them.
In Melbourne and Adelaide, trams share the road. You must stop behind a stationary tram when passengers are boarding or alighting unless there is a safety zone, and this is strictly enforced.

A minimum passing distance for cyclists applies in most states, generally one metre under sixty kilometres per hour and one and a half metres above it. Crossing a centre line to achieve it is permitted where safe.

sections.heading: Mobile phones and enforcement
body: Mobile phone laws are strict and enforced with dedicated detection cameras in several states. Touching a phone while driving, including while stationary in traffic, is an offence with substantial fines and demerit points.
Hands-free use through a cradle or Bluetooth is generally permitted for full licence holders but prohibited entirely for learner and provisional drivers. Set navigation before moving.
Fines are issued to the registered keeper, so a rental company will pass them on with an administration fee. Demerit points do not apply to overseas licences but the fines certainly do.
tips: Rentals pass on fines with a fee

sections.heading: Parking rules and signage
body: Parking signage in Australian cities is dense and strictly enforced, with clearways, permit zones, loading zones and time limits often stacked on one pole. Read the whole sign from the top down, because the most restrictive condition applies.

Clearways prohibit stopping entirely during posted hours and vehicles are towed rather than ticketed. In Sydney and Melbourne this catches visitors regularly and recovering a towed campervan is expensive and time consuming.
When unsure at an intersection, giving way costs a few seconds and resolves almost every uncertainty safely.
tips: Read the whole sign, top down

overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.title: Can you drive in Australia with an overseas licence?
overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.description: A state-by-state visitor guide to validity, translations, IDPs, vehicle class and conversion deadlines.
overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.imageAlt: Driver holding an overseas licence beside a rental vehicle
overseas-driver-licence-australia-state-.intro: There is no single nationwide deadline for driving on an overseas licence. Visitor status, residency, language, vehicle class and the state or territory all affect what documents and time limits apply.

sections.heading: Visitor rules are jurisdiction-specific
body: NSW temporary visitors can generally drive for up to six months when eligible, while Victoria also describes a six-month visitor period. Queensland and Western Australia use their own validity and residency rules.
Do not carry one state’s rule across a border. Open the authority page for every jurisdiction on the route.

sections.heading: Translations and document conditions
body: A non-English licence may require an approved English translation or International Driving Permit. Carry the physical documents required and obey every condition on the original licence.
An IDP supports the home licence; it does not replace an expired, suspended or otherwise invalid licence.

sections.heading: Vehicle class matters
body: A standard car class in NSW and Queensland generally covers no more than 4.5 tonnes GVM and 12 occupants including the driver. A larger motorhome may require a different authorised class.
Rental permission and insurance do not override licensing law. Confirm all three before accepting the vehicle.

sections.heading: Carrying the right documents
body: Carry the original overseas licence at all times, along with an English translation or International Driving Permit if it is not in English. The permit supports the licence rather than replacing it and both must be present.
Obtain the permit in your home country before travelling, because it generally cannot be issued after arrival. It is inexpensive and available from the relevant motoring authority.
Police can require both at a roadside stop, and being unable to produce them is an offence in its own right regardless of whether you are otherwise entitled to drive.
tips: Get the IDP before you travel
Failure to produce is an offence

sections.heading: Becoming a resident changes everything
body: The visitor periods apply to visitors. Once you become a resident of a state, the clock is different and conversion becomes mandatory within a defined period, frequently three months.

What counts as becoming a resident varies and can be triggered by a visa type, employment or simply length of stay. Working holiday visa holders in particular should check the position in the state they are living in.
Driving on an overseas licence after the residency deadline is driving unlicensed, with the insurance consequences that follow if anything happens.
tips: Past the deadline is unlicensed driving

sections.heading: Conditions and vehicle classes
body: Any condition on your original licence applies here: corrective lenses, automatic transmission only, or a graduated or probationary restriction. Driving outside those conditions is driving unlicensed.

A standard car class generally covers vehicles to 4.5 tonnes and twelve occupants, which covers most rental campervans but not all larger motorhomes. Check the vehicle specification against your class before booking.
Towing is assessed on the combination weight rather than the vehicle alone, so a car licence may not cover a heavy caravan behind a large four-wheel drive.
tips: 4.5 tonnes is the usual car limit
Towing is assessed on combined weight

sections.heading: What to do if you are stopped
body: Pull over promptly and safely, stay in the vehicle unless asked otherwise, and have your licence and any translation or permit ready. Random breath testing is routine and does not imply suspicion of anything.
Police in Australia are generally straightforward at roadside stops. Being unable to produce a licence is an offence in itself, so keeping the documents in the vehicle rather than in luggage matters.
Keep a photograph of every document stored separately from the originals, so a lost wallet is an inconvenience rather than the end of the driving.
tips: Failure to produce is an offence

australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.title: Australian road signs visitors should know
australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.description: Regulatory, warning, advisory and roadwork signs explained for people starting an Australian road trip.
australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.imageAlt: Australian warning and regulatory road signs
australian-road-signs-visitors-guide.intro: Australian signs use familiar shapes and colours, but a visitor needs to distinguish a legal instruction from a hazard warning or advisory speed. Temporary traffic control matters just as much as a permanent sign.

sections.heading: Regulatory signs
body: Stop, Give Way, speed limit, Keep Left, No Entry, prohibited turns, roundabouts and shared zones create legal requirements. A Stop sign requires a complete stop.
Give Way requires slowing and stopping when necessary, then applying the priority rule for the intersection.

sections.heading: Warnings and advisory speeds
body: Warning signs identify bends, merging or narrowing lanes, animals, unsealed surfaces, floodways and railway crossings. The hazard changes how you drive even when the posted maximum stays the same.
A regulatory speed sign is not the same as an advisory speed displayed for a bend or crest. Slow to the conditions and vehicle.
tips: Do not treat advisory speed as a target

sections.heading: Roadworks and road trains
body: Temporary speed limits, traffic lights and traffic-controller directions at roadworks must be obeyed. Conditions can change between trips.
A yellow ROAD TRAIN or LONG VEHICLE panel attached to a truck identifies that vehicle. Give it space; do not mistake the panel for a roadside direction.

sections.heading: Signs you will not have seen elsewhere
body: Floodway markers with depth indicators appear on roads that cross watercourses, and the numbered posts show water depth. Never enter if the depth is unknown or the water is moving.
Grid signs warn of cattle grids, which can be rough at speed. Open range and stock warning signs indicate unfenced roads where animals may be on the carriageway at any time.
Road train and long vehicle signs on trucks identify combinations up to 53.5 metres. The sign is attached to the vehicle rather than being a roadside instruction, which confuses many visitors.
tips: Road train signs are on the truck

sections.heading: Speed signage and variable limits
body: Speed limits are in kilometres per hour and the default open road limit varies by state, from 100 in most to 110 on many highways and 130 on specified Northern Territory sections.
Variable message signs and electronic speed signs override posted limits and are common around roadworks, tunnels and school zones. Roadwork limits apply whether or not work is visibly happening.
Advisory speeds on yellow signs at corners are not legal limits but are set for a car in good conditions. In a loaded campervan or towing, the safe speed is lower again.
tips: Default open limits vary by state
Yellow advisory signs assume a car

sections.heading: Wildlife and fatigue signage
body: Animal warning signs indicating kangaroos, wombats, cassowaries or camels mark areas with genuine strike risk, concentrated around dawn and dusk. Treat them as a reason to reduce speed rather than decoration.
Driver reviver and rest area signs mark places to stop for fatigue, and on long routes the distance to the next one is often shown. Use them rather than pushing on.
Some remote routes carry signs stating the distance to the next fuel or water. Those are not suggestions; on the Nullarbor and through the outback they are the information your trip depends on.
tips: Animal signs mark real strike zones
Rest area signs show the next distance

sections.heading: Distance markers and location signs
body: Roadside distance markers and location reference signs are how you describe where you are to emergency services in remote areas. Noting the nearest one before making a call saves a great deal of time.

Many highways carry signs showing the distance to the next fuel, water or rest area. On outback routes these are planning information rather than trivia, and they are frequently the most useful signs on the road.
Spend ten minutes with a signs guide before the first driving day, because recognising an unfamiliar sign at speed is considerably harder than learning it in advance.
tips: Note markers before calling for help
Fuel distance signs are planning data

campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.title: Campervan driving in Australia: size, safety and legal limits
campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.description: Check licence class, vehicle dimensions, restraints and road exclusions before the first long driving day.
campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.imageAlt: Campervan travelling on an Australian highway
campervan-driving-australia-safety-guide.intro: A campervan may feel like a large car until braking, crosswind or a low branch exposes its real size. The safe handover begins with dimensions, loaded weight, licence class and rental conditions.

sections.heading: Know the vehicle before moving
body: Record the height, length and GVM, locate the fuel type and learn the mirrors, blind spots and controls. A vehicle above 4.5 tonnes may fall outside an ordinary car licence.
Confirm tyre, awning, roof, gas and interior stowage procedures with the operator.

sections.heading: Everyone travels in a proper seat
body: Beds and living areas are not passenger positions while moving. Every occupant must use an approved seat and the required restraint.
Secure loose items before every drive. A cupboard or bottle becomes dangerous under sudden braking.

sections.heading: Drive for the loaded vehicle
body: Allow more stopping distance, turn smoothly and slow before bends, gravel, crosswinds and narrow shoulders. A legal maximum can still be unsafe.
Rental exclusions, insurance conditions and government road rules are separate requirements. Permission from one does not cancel the others.

sections.heading: Wind, road trains and overtaking
body: A high-sided campervan catches crosswind badly, and a passing road train produces a significant push followed by a pull. Hold the wheel firmly with both hands and do not correct sharply.
Overtaking in a campervan requires far more clear road than a car needs, and most Australian highways are two-lane with limited passing lanes. If an overtake feels marginal, do not attempt it.
When traffic builds behind you, use the next slow vehicle bay and let it past. Frustrated following drivers cause overtaking crashes, and removing that pressure is both courteous and safer for you.

sections.heading: Unsealed roads and what your agreement allows
body: Most standard rental agreements prohibit unsealed roads entirely or name specific exclusions, with damage on them uninsured. Vehicles are tracked, so driving them anyway is not a private decision.
On gravel, reduce speed well below sealed-road pace, brake and steer gently and separately, and leave a very large gap behind anything raising dust. Windscreen damage is the most common claim.
Lowering tyre pressures for corrugations improves comfort and reduces damage, but you must reinflate before returning to sealed roads. Carry a gauge and a compressor if you intend to do this.
tips: Huge gap behind anything raising dust

sections.heading: Heat, tyres and vehicle checks
body: Australian heat is hard on tyres, and underinflated or old tyres fail at speed on hot bitumen. Check pressures cold, set them for the loaded vehicle, and inspect the spare before a remote leg.
Check coolant, oil and washer levels regularly, particularly before long outback legs. A breakdown in remote heat is a safety problem rather than an inconvenience.
Carry more water than the trip requires. If the vehicle stops in remote country, water is what keeps the situation manageable while you wait, and you should always wait with the vehicle.
tips: Check the spare before remote legs

sections.heading: Parking and manoeuvring in towns
body: Height restrictions in urban car parks are the most common source of expensive campervan damage, and the barrier is usually the first warning. Write the vehicle height somewhere visible from the driver's seat and check every entrance.
Many towns provide oversized vehicle parking on the outskirts or at showgrounds. Using it and walking in is faster than circling a town centre looking for a space that fits.
Do a full walk around the vehicle each morning, checking tyres, lights and that nothing is left on the roof or open underneath.
tips: Write the height on the dashboard
Car park barriers are the first warning

towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.title: Towing a caravan in Australia: weights, speed and state differences
towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.description: A practical guide to loaded limits, couplings, braking room and the towing rules that change at state borders.
towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.imageAlt: Car and caravan travelling on an Australian road
towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.intro: Safe towing starts with the actual loaded combination, not the empty caravan brochure. Manufacturer limits, ball load, licence conditions and jurisdiction rules all need to agree.

sections.heading: Weights and connection
body: Keep the loaded caravan within the tow vehicle, towbar, coupling and manufacturer limits. Secure the load and inspect chains, hatches, tyres, brakes and lights.
Repeat the inspection during long trips. Heat, vibration and rough surfaces can expose a problem that was not visible at departure.

sections.heading: Nobody rides in the caravan
body: A towed caravan or trailer is not a passenger compartment. Everyone travels in an approved vehicle seating position with the correct restraint.
Extra length and mass require longer stopping distance, wider cornering lines and smooth steering and braking.

sections.heading: Speed rules vary
body: Western Australia limits a vehicle towing a trailer or caravan to 100 km/h and has a 60-metre following rule behind certain heavy or towing vehicles unless overtaking.
NSW’s cited 100 km/h cap applies when the towing vehicle or combination exceeds 4.5 tonnes. Never turn one jurisdiction’s rule into a nationwide towing speed.

sections.heading: Reversing, parking and campgrounds
body: Practise reversing in an empty car park before the trip. Caravan park sites frequently require a reverse into a defined space with neighbours close on both sides, and doing it for the first time with an audience is how vans get damaged.
Book sites suited to your combination length and say you are towing when booking. Many parks keep drive-through sites, which removes most of the difficulty from arrival.
Unhitching gives you an ordinary vehicle for day trips and is worth doing on any stay longer than one night. Use wheel chocks and levelling ramps and check the handbrake holds first.
tips: Unhitch for stays over one night

sections.heading: Roads and conditions to avoid
body: Many mountain and coastal roads are unsuitable for large combinations, and some are prohibited outright. Check before committing, because turning a caravan around on a narrow road is frequently impossible.
On descents, select a lower gear and use engine braking rather than riding the brakes, which fade and can fail entirely on a long grade with a heavy van behind.
Unsealed roads with corrugations are hard on caravans and cause structural damage over time. Many insurance policies exclude or limit cover for damage sustained on them.

sections.heading: Weights and the paperwork that matters
body: The limiting figure is whichever is lowest of the tow vehicle's capacity, the towbar rating, the caravan's aggregate trailer mass and the tow ball rating. Exceeding any of them affects handling, braking and insurance.
Weigh the loaded combination rather than estimating. Public weighbridges are widely available and inexpensive, and most caravans travel heavier than their owners believe.
Keep around ten percent of the weight on the tow ball and load heavy items low and over the axle. Rear-loading a caravan is the most common cause of sway.
tips: Ten percent on the tow ball

sections.heading: Before every driving day
body: Walk around the combination: check the coupling is latched and pinned, safety chains are crossed and connected, the jockey wheel is up, lights and brakes work, and nothing is loose on the drawbar or roof.
Repeat a quick check at the first stop of the day. Heat, vibration and corrugations loosen fittings, and a problem found at a fuel stop is trivial compared with the same problem found at speed.
Consider a towing course before a first long trip, since a day of instruction covers reversing, weight distribution and sway recovery far better than reading about them.

driving-with-road-trains-australia.title: How to share Australian roads with road trains
driving-with-road-trains-australia.description: Overtaking, dust, stopping distance and single-lane-road behaviour around vehicles up to 60 metres long.
driving-with-road-trains-australia.imageAlt: Road train on a remote Australian highway
driving-with-road-trains-australia.intro: A road train can be roughly 27.5 to 60 metres long. It needs space to stop, turn and pass, and the safest driver is predictable rather than helpful in an improvised way.

sections.heading: Following and overtaking
body: Stay well back, especially on unsealed roads where dust can erase visibility. Never pass without a long, fully visible clear stretch.
Do not overtake a turning road train or cut in after passing. Its stopping distance is much greater than a car’s.

sections.heading: When a road train passes you
body: Northern Territory guidance says to maintain speed and keep left, then slow only once the truck has moved out to pass. Sudden early slowing can disrupt the manoeuvre.
Do not rely on informal flashing lights or UHF directions as if they were legal traffic control.

sections.heading: Single-lane and unsealed roads
body: On an NT single-lane highway, slow and pull off, moving slowly on the shoulder for an approaching road train when safe. Expect dust and loose stones.
Choose a safe place and avoid a soft, steep or damaged shoulder. Conditions and jurisdiction guidance still control the decision.

sections.heading: Where you will meet them
body: Road trains operate across the Northern Territory, outback Queensland, northern South Australia and much of Western Australia, with the longest combinations on designated routes. Triples and quads are normal on those roads.

They are also present on approach roads to mines and cattle stations, frequently on unsealed surfaces where dust makes them nearly invisible until close. Assume they may be around any blind corner on a station road.
Their length means they cannot stop, swerve or move over meaningfully. Every safety decision on these roads is yours to make rather than theirs.
tips: They cannot swerve or stop quickly

sections.heading: Overtaking one safely
body: You need a very long, fully visible clear stretch, considerably more than for a truck at home. Judging the length of a road train from behind is difficult, and misjudging it is the classic fatal error on these roads.
Never begin an overtake on a crest, a curve or where dust limits visibility. If you cannot see the entire combination and a long clear road beyond it, wait.
Once past, do not cut back in early. Their stopping distance is far greater than a car's, and pulling in close in front removes the only margin they have.
tips: You need far more clear road
Never overtake into dust or a crest
Do not cut in close after passing

sections.heading: When one is passing you or approaching
body: When a road train overtakes, maintain your speed and hold your line to the left. Slowing suddenly disrupts the manoeuvre and lengthens the time it spends on the wrong side of the road.
On single-lane bitumen, common in the outback, slow down and move onto the shoulder for an approaching road train, keeping both left wheels off the seal. Expect flying stones and a large dust cloud.
On unsealed roads, pull well over and stop if visibility will disappear. Waiting thirty seconds for dust to clear is the correct response, not driving blind through it.
tips: Hold speed and line when passed
Move off single-lane seal for oncoming
Stop and wait for dust to clear

sections.heading: Road trains at roadhouses and rest areas
body: Roadhouses are working stops for road train drivers, and the parking areas are laid out for vehicles that cannot easily reverse or turn. Park clear of the truck bays and the entry and exit lines.

Drivers are on regulated rest breaks and the parking bays exist for that. Blocking them is both inconsiderate and creates a genuine safety issue when a driver has to move a fifty metre combination around a badly parked van.
A UHF radio on channel 40 lets you hear truck drivers discussing conditions ahead, which is genuinely useful information on remote highways.
tips: Drivers are on mandated rest breaks
Keep entry and exit lines clear

australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.title: Fatigue, wildlife and night driving on Australian road trips
australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.description: Recognise fatigue early, plan real breaks and reduce the risk of dawn, dusk and remote-road driving.
australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.imageAlt: Kangaroo beside a quiet Australian road at dusk
australia-road-trip-fatigue-wildlife-saf.intro: Long distances do not make fatigue inevitable; tight itineraries do. Sleep is the only cure, wildlife is harder to see around dawn and dusk, and a daylight arrival gives every backup more room.

sections.heading: Recognise fatigue before it becomes a crisis
body: Yawning, heavy eyes, lane drift, forgotten kilometres and inconsistent speed are warnings to stop. Music, open windows and caffeine do not replace sleep.
Plan a break at least every two hours. Victorian guidance recommends no more than eight hours of driving in a 24-hour period.

sections.heading: Wildlife and night
body: Animals and livestock are particularly active around dawn and dusk. Reduce speed when animals are near the road and avoid swerving, which can cause a rollover or another collision.
Prefer daylight on unfamiliar roads and finish before fatigue begins choosing the speed, lane position or next stop.

sections.heading: Remote breakdown preparation
body: Carry extra water, food, fuel margin and an appropriate communication method where services are sparse. Tell someone the route and expected arrival.
Official WA remote-travel guidance says to remain with the vehicle if stranded. A vehicle provides shelter and is easier for rescuers to find.

sections.heading: Why distances here cause fatigue
body: Australian driving involves long, straight, monotonous roads with little to react to, which produces highway hypnosis far more readily than winding roads do. The absence of stimulus is itself the hazard.

Fatigue is a factor in a substantial share of regional crashes, and it accumulates across days rather than resetting overnight. A week of long driving days leaves you impaired even after a full night's sleep.
Plan the itinerary so no day requires more than about four hours of driving, and build in days where nobody drives at all. Most fatigue problems are planning problems.

sections.heading: Recognising it too late
body: Yawning, heavy eyes, drifting within the lane, missing a turn and having no memory of the last stretch are late signs. By the time you notice them, reaction time is already substantially impaired.
Stop every two hours as a rule rather than when you feel tired. A twenty minute nap is genuinely effective; coffee, music, open windows and conversation mask symptoms while the impairment continues.
Driver reviver stops and rest areas exist across the country for exactly this. Use them rather than treating a planned arrival time as fixed.
tips: Stop every two hours by rule
Coffee masks, it does not fix

sections.heading: Animals and the case against driving at night
body: Kangaroos, wombats, cattle, camels and emus are most active from dusk to dawn and are drawn to roadside vegetation. A strike at highway speed disables a vehicle and in remote areas that becomes a serious situation.
Do not drive between dusk and dawn in rural Australia if you can avoid it. This single decision removes most of the animal strike risk and much of the fatigue risk at once.
If an animal is on the road, brake in a straight line rather than swerving. Swerving is what turns a strike into a rollover, and in a high-sided vehicle the rollover risk is significant.
tips: Do not drive dusk to dawn
A strike in remote country is serious

sections.heading: If you do hit an animal
body: Stop when safe, and move the vehicle off the road. Do not approach a large injured animal such as a kangaroo or a wombat, because a distressed animal can cause serious injury with its hind legs or claws.

Call the relevant state wildlife rescue service, which can be reached from most areas with coverage. In marsupial country, checking a female's pouch is worth doing only if you are trained; otherwise report the location and let rescuers handle it.
Share the driving where you can, and treat the second driver as a real part of the plan rather than a backup who never actually drives.

australia-road-rules-state-differences.title: Australian road rules that change across states and territories
australia-road-rules-state-differences.description: Default speeds, towing, devices and licence conditions compared without turning local rules into national advice.
australia-road-rules-state-differences.imageAlt: Australian highway crossing a state border
australia-road-rules-state-differences.intro: Australian road rules are broadly consistent, but the legislation belongs to each state and territory. Default speeds, mobile-device exceptions, provisional restrictions, towing and overseas-licence periods can change at a border.

sections.heading: Model rules and local law
body: The Australian Road Rules provide a national model. Jurisdictions enact and amend their own versions, so a summary cannot replace the current local authority.
Posted signs, licence conditions and lower vehicle-specific limits always take priority over a general default.

sections.heading: Default unsigned speed examples
body: Queensland and Victoria describe 50 km/h in built-up areas and 100 km/h outside built-up areas. Western Australia states 50 km/h built-up and 110 km/h on open roads.
The Northern Territory generally uses 60 km/h in built-up areas unless gazetted lower and 110 km/h outside, with signed 130 km/h sections on specified highways.

sections.heading: The other differences that matter
body: Mobile-device exceptions, learner and provisional conditions, towing speeds and overseas-licence conversion periods all vary. A rental company can also impose tighter road exclusions.
Save direct state authority links before travel and review them whenever the vehicle, licence status or jurisdiction changes.

sections.heading: Why the rules differ at all
body: Road law in Australia is made by each state and territory rather than nationally. The Australian Road Rules provide a model that jurisdictions adopt with variations, so the base is consistent and the details are not.
The practical consequence is that speed defaults, mobile device exceptions, towing limits, licence conditions and even some signage change as you cross a border, frequently with no reminder.
On a trip crossing several states this matters. Check the position in each jurisdiction on your route rather than carrying one state's rules across the whole country.
tips: Each state makes its own road law
Borders change the rules without warning
Check each jurisdiction on the route

sections.heading: The differences most likely to catch you
body: Default open road limits vary from 100 to 110 kilometres per hour, with specified Northern Territory sections at 130. Built-up area defaults also differ, with the Territory using 60 rather than 50.
Towing speed limits differ, with Western Australia capping towing at 100 and other states applying limits based on vehicle mass. Following distance rules behind heavy vehicles also vary.
Mobile phone rules, learner and provisional restrictions and the treatment of overseas licences all differ between states, and the penalties for getting them wrong are real.

sections.heading: Crossing borders in practice
body: Quarantine checkpoints operate at several state borders, restricting fresh produce, honey, plants and soil. These are enforced with fines and, at some crossings, detector dogs.

Time zones change at some borders and not others, and several states observe daylight saving while others do not. Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia do not, which creates larger gaps in summer.
Fuel prices, alcohol restrictions and even the availability of particular fuel grades change across borders. Check what applies where you are going rather than where you have been.

sections.heading: Practical border checklist
body: Before each border, run through the short list: quarantine produce, time zone change, fuel top-up, alcohol restrictions ahead, and any change to speed or towing limits. It takes two minutes and prevents most border problems.
Save the relevant state road authority page for each jurisdiction on your route while you have reception. Rules change and the authority page is the only source that reflects the current position.
When in doubt, follow the stricter rule you know of. It is never an offence to drive more cautiously than the local limit permits.
tips: Run a border checklist each time
